keywords: Flip over / flip (noun) / somersault invertō, invertere; saltus cernuus invertō, invertere, invertī, inversum — turn something over or upside down; transitive. sē invertere — turn oneself over; the verb is also attested with a reflexive object. cernuō, cernuāre — do a somersault; recorded by Morgan–Owens, including an Apuleius reference. saltus cernuus; saltūs cernuī m. — somersault / acrobatic flip; singular nominative and genitive. Morgan–Owens lists the plural saltūs cernuī ; the singular is inflected here from that expression. Tabulam inverte. — Flip the plank over. Saltum cernuum fac. — Do a somersault. These distinguish turning an object over from a bodily flip. They do not imply that a coin toss, switch operation, cartwheel and airborne backflip all have the same exact technical name. keywords: Squeeze / squish / squash / crush comprimō, comprimere; contundō, contundere comprimō, comprimere, compressī, compressum — squeeze or press together, compress. Our practical choice for squishing something soft or squashing it down; the object supplies the soft/wet quality. exprimō, exprimere, expressī, expressum — squeeze liquid out; also wring out the object containing it. Spongiam exprime. — Squeeze out the sponge. See also the food-preparation squeeze entry. contundō, contundere, contudī, contūsum — pound, mash or crush by blows; Lewis & Short includes olives, roots and crushing/flattening injuries. The perfect has recorded quantity variation; contudī is left without a root-vowel macron here. conterō, conterere, contrīvī, contrītum — grind or crush into small pieces; already covered in the cooking entry as well. Lūtum comprime. — Squish / compress the mud. Spongiam nōlī comprimere. — Don’t squeeze the sponge. English “squeeze,” “squish,” “squash” and “crush” overlap. These Latin choices distinguish compression, extraction, pounding and grinding; they are not four rigid one-to-one equivalents. keywords: Crash (verb) / crash (noun) / collision / crashing sound collīdō, collīdere; collīsiō, collīsiōnis f. collīdō, collīdere, collīsī, collīsum — dash or strike things together; transitive. To describe objects colliding, use the passive collīdī , with inter sē when appropriate. collīsiō, collīsiōnis f. — collision; Morgan–Owens records the automobile application, citing Traupman. It also records collīsus, collīsūs m. with a Vatican Lexicon reference. fragor, fragōris m. — crash or crashing sound; distinguishes the noise from the collision itself. corruō, corruere, corruī — fall or collapse; useful when “crash” means coming down in a heap rather than hitting another object. Traupman also applies it to a computer crash; that is a separate modern extension. Autoraedae inter sē collīduntur. — The cars crash into each other. Magnum fragōrem audīvī. — I heard a loud crash. For toy cars the vehicle nouns have modern applications; the sentence is our composed description, not an ancient quotation.
